This ZIP specifies an off-chain channel between Zcash wallets. A Sender wallet that holds a Recipient wallet’s Unified Address deposits an encrypted Envelope in a Mailbox over an anonymity network, and the Recipient wallet fetches it later. Neither wallet reveals its network identity to the other, and the Mailbox operator does not learn who sent an Envelope.

Envelopes are encrypted to the Orchard Receiver of the Unified Address, using the Orchard key agreement with a domain-separated key derivation, so no new keys have to be exchanged. A new ZIP 316 Metadata Item carries the Mailbox Descriptor in the Unified Address. Payload types are defined for acknowledgements, text, ZIP 321 payment requests, and PCZTs, with codes reserved for FROST signing rounds and off-chain note delivery. Mailbox credentials are derived from the wallet seed with ZIP 32 registered key derivation.

Anyone who holds the recipient’s Orchard incoming viewing key can read its Envelopes, and a Mailbox Descriptor links every Unified Address that carries it. Transport Bindings are specified separately; Appendix A sketches one for the Nym mixnet.
Several wallet protocols need a direct channel between wallets. Each wallet that wants one currently builds its own, so wallets from different vendors cannot talk to each other:
Multisig and hardware-signer flows pass PCZTs

) runs over a confidential, authenticated channel between the Coordinator and the signers whose mechanism ZIP 312 leaves out of scope. This ZIP supplies the confidential, anonymous transport; a FROST payload would have to carry its own authentication.
) and acknowledgements have no wallet-to-wallet transport.
proposes removing in-band secret distribution from transactions, which makes an off-chain delivery channel a requirement rather than an add-on.
On-chain memos are the only standard channel today. ZIP 231

proposes to lift their 512-byte size cap, but memos would still cost fees, be stored by every full validator forever, and need a block confirmation per round, which rules out interactive protocols such as PCZT and FROST exchanges.

delegates delivery to a channel the parties already share, such as a secure messenger or a QR code, for the case where the sender has no address for the recipient. It does not help when the sender does hold a Unified Address, which is the case this ZIP covers.
The idea is not new. Hornby’s 2020 light wallet privacy review
lists out-of-band transaction delivery over a mixnet as an option and notes that scalable Zcash will need a mixnet or similar technology anyway. zips#629
suggests a mixnet plus a “private mailbox” to keep offline reception. The Nym × Zcash integration guide
covers routing a wallet’s chain-sync and transaction-submission traffic through the mixnet, not wallet-to-wallet delivery. This ZIP fills that gap.

Envelopes are encrypted to an Orchard Receiver, so anyone holding the account’s Orchard incoming viewing key can decrypt them. That is the trust model of incoming notes, but Envelopes can carry more: a PCZT reveals a transaction the recipient is about to sign, including its outputs. Users who share incoming viewing keys with auditors or watch-only services should not expect Envelopes to be private from them.

A Mailbox Descriptor is a stable identifier. Two Unified Addresses that carry the same descriptor are linked to one recipient by anyone who sees both, which defeats diversified addresses. Unlinkable addresses therefore need separate mailboxes, at the cost of more credentials to derive and more mailboxes to fetch from. A
address inside an Envelope has the same property for the sender.
Network observers and the Mailbox operator.

The anonymity network hides the sender’s network identity from the operator and the recipient, and the recipient’s from the sender. The operator still sees how many Envelopes a mailbox receives, their size classes, and when they are deposited and fetched. In bindings where the recipient connects to its own mailbox directly, as in the Nym sketch of Appendix A, the operator also learns the recipient’s network identity unless the connection is tunnelled, for example over Tor. Network privacy is only as good as the anonymity set: while few wallets use a binding, cover traffic carries most of the weight.

A deposit made at the same moment as a related on-chain broadcast, a fetch triggered by opening the app, or an immediate acknowledgement each leak timing that an observer can correlate with chain activity. The wallet behaviour rules in the specification reduce but do not remove this.
No sender authentication and no forward secrecy.

Envelopes do not authenticate their sender, so a Text payload can impersonate anyone; the specification forbids presenting it as coming from a named party. Envelope keys derive from long-lived keys, so compromise of an incoming viewing key exposes every Envelope the adversary has recorded, as for on-chain notes.

Anyone holding a Unified Address can fill its mailbox. The cost falls on the mailbox’s storage and the recipient’s bandwidth; trial decryption itself is cheap. Bindings are expected to document quotas, and the unencrypted Envelope header lets a wallet see size classes before fetching bodies where a binding allows that.
A sender holding only a recipient’s Unified Address can deliver a message with no prior contact.
The recipient need not be online when the message is sent.
No long-term key material is needed beyond what the wallet derives from its seed, and a wallet restored from seed can recover its mailboxes on a best-effort basis.
Neither the Mailbox operator nor a network observer learns the sender’s network identity or links a sender to a recipient. The sender does not learn the recipient’s network identity.
An Envelope reveals nothing about its content beyond its size class.

Wallets that implement ZIP 316 but not this ZIP can still parse and pay a Unified Address that carries a Mailbox Descriptor, provided the Typecode registration requested in the Specification is granted.
The core protocol does not depend on any one network or token.
Sender authentication at the Envelope layer. Payload types that need it carry their own.
Guaranteed delivery. Delivery is best-effort; protocols built on top have to handle loss.
Hiding the recipient’s network identity from its own Mailbox operator. A binding may provide this, and a wallet can add Tor, but the core does not require it.

A Transport Binding MUST provide these operations:
(descriptor, envelope): deliver an Envelope to the Mailbox named by the descriptor.
(credential, handles): remove fetched Envelopes, unless the binding documents that Fetch removes them implicitly.

A Transport Binding MUST hide the sender’s network identity from the Mailbox operator and from the recipient, and MUST hide the recipient’s network identity from the sender. It SHOULD hide the recipient’s network identity from the Mailbox operator, and SHOULD resist timing correlation by a global passive adversary. Bindings SHOULD rate-limit Deposit and SHOULD bound the storage a mailbox can consume.

Wallets SHOULD NOT deposit an Envelope at the same moment as a related on-chain broadcast, and SHOULD add a random delay when the use is not interactive.
Wallets MUST NOT fall back to a direct connection to a Mailbox when the binding’s anonymity network is unavailable.
Wallets SHOULD fetch on a randomized schedule that does not depend on user actions, including when no message is expected.
Wallets SHOULD cap the bytes they fetch and trial-decrypt per Fetch.

Envelopes are not authenticated. Wallets MUST NOT present a message as coming from a named party unless the payload type itself authenticates the sender, and SHOULD NOT open links in Text payloads without user confirmation.
Wallets that export an account’s incoming viewing key to a third party SHOULD NOT advertise mailboxes on that account’s addresses.

It needs no new keys and no prior contact: any Unified Address with an Orchard Receiver is already a public encryption key. The cost is that incoming viewing key holders can read Envelopes; a dedicated messaging key in the descriptor would avoid that at the cost of a larger Item.
Exact lengths would leak payload types and content. Three classes keep the anonymity set per class large while still allowing PCZTs.
A sender that can use this channel already holds the recipient’s Unified Address and can pay it on chain, and a ZIP 324 URI carries spend authority that every incoming viewing key holder could use.

Tying a standard to one network and its token is a long-term risk. Nym is sketched first because it is live, packet-based, uses cover traffic, stores messages for offline clients, and offers sender-anonymous replies.

Whether to encrypt to a dedicated messaging key carried in the descriptor instead of to the Orchard Receiver, so that incoming viewing key holders cannot read Envelopes.

Address Expiry Items make an address unpayable by ZIP 316 Revision 0 Consumers, while the compatibility requirement assumes they can pay it. Whether to recommend expiry, shorter-lived descriptors, or neither.

This appendix sketches a binding for the Nym mixnet so that the core protocol can be evaluated against a real network. It is not a complete Transport Binding specification: the items marked TBD have to be resolved before it can be made normative.

would be the Ed25519 seed of the client identity key, and the last 32 bytes the X25519 secret key
of the client encryption key. The Nym Rust SDK accepts externally supplied client keys through a custom key store.

The sender sends the Envelope as a Nym message to the descriptor’s address through the mixnet, from an ephemeral Nym client with fresh keys rather than from its own mailbox client, attaching reply SURBs
if it expects a prompt reply. Each ephemeral client has to register with an entry gateway and hold bandwidth credentials; the cost and latency of doing so per message are unverified (TBD).

The recipient runs a Nym client with the derived keys, connected to the gateway named in the descriptor, with cover traffic on. The gateway stores messages while the client is offline and delivers them when it connects.
Implicit on delivery by the gateway (TBD: confirm).
All. Nym splits a message into fixed-size Sphinx packets, so larger classes take more packets and leave a larger timing footprint.
SURB reply keys expire after 24 hours,
so SURBs serve interactive exchanges only. A recipient that fetches later can reply only to a
address that carries a Nym descriptor.
Sending through Nym consumes bandwidth credentials. Who pays, and whether they can be bought with shielded ZEC, is TBD.

The gateway is part of the descriptor. If the recipient moves gateway, old descriptors stop working and a new Unified Address has to be issued. How a wallet restored from seed learns which gateway each mailbox index used is TBD.

The recipient’s gateway, which is the Mailbox operator, sees the recipient’s connection, including its IP address unless the connection is tunnelled over Tor, and the count and size of stored messages. The sender’s entry gateway sees the sender’s IP address but not the destination. Mix nodes see packets only. A global passive adversary faces Nym’s mixing delays and cover traffic.
